Launched
läncht
v. (put a vessel out from shore; set sail — Greek anago, to put out to sea)
Old French lancier, to throw or hurl, from Latin lancea, a lance. To launch is to thrust a vessel out from the land.

Biblical Definition

Launched is the Authorized Version's word for putting out from shore, and it marks the beginning of several decisive passages. On the lake: “he went into a ship with his disciples: and he said unto them, Let us go over unto the other side of the lake. And they launched forth” (Luk 8:22) — and the storm that followed was the occasion of His rebuking the wind and the raging of the water. At Peter's call: “when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught” (Luk 5:4) — a carpenter telling a fisherman where the fish were, after a night of nothing, and Peter's answer was nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net. In Acts the word carries Paul toward Rome: “entering into a ship of Adramyttium, we launched, meaning to sail by the coasts of Asia” (Act 27:2), and “when we had launched from thence, we sailed under Cyprus, because the winds were contrary” (Act 27:4). Every one of these launchings ran into weather. The Lord slept through one, stilled it, and asked where their faith was; Peter's obedient launch filled two ships to sinking; Paul's voyage ended in shipwreck on Melita with every soul saved, exactly as the angel had told him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines launch as to move or cause to slide from the land into the water; to put out to sea; to begin a new course or enterprise.

expand to see more

LAUNCH, v.t. To throw, as a lance; to move or cause to slide from the land into the water; as, to launch a ship.

2. To put out; to send on a course; as, to launch into the deep.

LAUNCH, v.i. To glide, as a ship into the water; to put out to sea; to enter on a new field of activity.

DEEP, n. The sea; the abyss of waters; the ocean.

Key Scripture

Luke 8:22 — "Now it came to pass on a certain day, that he went into a ship with his disciples: and he said unto them, Let us go over unto the other side of the lake. And they launched forth."

Luke 5:4 — "Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught."

Acts 27:2 — "And entering into a ship of Adramyttium, we launched, meaning to sail by the coasts of Asia; one Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us."

Acts 27:4 — "And when we had launched from thence, we sailed under Cyprus, because the winds were contrary."

Modern Corruption

Obedience is expected to produce calm passage, and a storm on the way is read as evidence that the launch was a mistake.

expand to see more

Luke 8 is decisive on this point and is regularly ignored. It was the Lord who said let us go over unto the other side, and the boat that went at His word ran into a storm that frightened professional fishermen. Obedience did not prevent the weather; it appointed the meeting. The disciples' error was not in launching but in concluding, when the water came in, that He did not care — carest thou not that we perish? — and His question afterwards was not why they were afraid of the sea but where is your faith? A believer in trouble on a course God gave him is exactly where he ought to be.

Peter's launch adds the other half. He had toiled all night and taken nothing, and he was being told where to fish by a carpenter, in the middle of the day, in deep water, in front of a crowd. His reply is the model of obedient faith: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net. He did not say he expected fish; he said he would do it because of who was speaking. The nets broke and the ships began to sink, and Peter's response was to fall down and say, depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. That is the usual order — obedience first, evidence second, and self-knowledge last of all.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anago (G321), to lead up, put out to sea — Luke 8:22, Acts 27:2, 27:4; epanago (G1877), to put out further — Luke 5:3-4; bathos (G899), the deep.

expand to see more

Greek anago (G321) — to put out to sea, set sail; Luke 8:22, Acts 13:13, Acts 27:2 and 27:4.

Greek epanago (G1877) — to put out further from shore; Luke 5:3 of thrusting out a little, 5:4 of launching into the deep.

Greek bathos (G899) — depth, the deep; Luke 5:4, and Romans 11:33 of the depth of the riches of God.

Greek chalao (G5465) — to let down; the nets in Luke 5:4-5.

Every launching in these passages met weather, and none of them was a mistake.

Usage

"“Let us go over unto the other side… and they launched forth” — straight into the storm."

"“Launch out into the deep” — a carpenter to a fisherman, at the wrong hour."

"“The winds were contrary” — and the voyage was still God's."
